title: Sleep
hookLine: a soft bed and a sleepless night, and a teacher who slept well on leaves in the frost
tomorrow: can stopping be part of trying, not its opposite?

lines: A GOOD BED, A WIDE-AWAKE MIND.
cards: A good mattress, blackout curtains, a sleep app with rain sounds, and still the eyes open at three in the morning, the mind running laps around tomorrow's worries and yesterday's words.
A householder named Hatthaka once found the Buddha outdoors on a winter night, sitting on a thin spread of leaves beside a cattle path, with frost on the ground. Hatthaka asked: did you sleep well?
And the Buddha, on that cold ground, said yes, without a hint of complaint. He was one of those in the world who sleep well.

teach.h: A FEVER A BED CAN'T COOL.
teach.b: Hatthaka can't believe it. The night is cold, the leaves are thin, the wind is sharp. So the Buddha turns the question around.
Picture a rich man in a fine house, on a soft couch with warm covers.
Could a fever of wanting keep him awake? Of anger? Of confusion?
Yes, says Hatthaka. Those fevers, the Buddha says, are gone in me, so I sleep well, even here. A bed can't cool a fever in the mind; only the mind's own letting go can do that.
That's not a reason to sleep on frost; it's a reason to look at what we carry to bed.
And this week has given us tools for exactly that. Now a round with the six lines behind us. Guard the door: mindfulness at six open gates.
Put it down: the hand left empty a moment longer. Quiet at home: made, not found. Food with care: like medicine on a wound.
A little less: the king's verse at every meal. As your own eyes: the cook's rice and water.
Each one, in its way, cools a fever before night comes: less grabbing, less noise, a body fed with care.
Six lines, and a bed of leaves starts to look less strange.

how: Many Buddhists end the day with a few minutes of metta, wishing beings well, and the suttas recommend lying down mindfully, noting the intention to rise.

o: rest that comes when the mind's fevers have cooled
a deep trance that replaces a night's rest
a vow to rest only a few hours each night

games.q: the happy sleeper — tap the pairs.
p: asked if the Buddha slept well
a fever a soft bed can't cool

s: the Buddha told Hatthaka to sleep on frozen ground
he explained why he slept well: the fevers of the mind were gone.
in the sutta, a rich man on a soft couch can still lie awake
a fever of wanting, anger or confusion can keep him up.
guarding the senses means bricking the gates shut
the gates stay open; mindfulness stands at them and chooses.

games.q: you can't sleep, replaying a fight from dinner. by Hatthaka's story, what would help most?
o: a better pillow and a white-noise app.
cool the fever: notice the anger, and wish the other person well.
get up and finish the argument by text.
games.why: the Buddha said a soft bed can't cool a fever of anger; he slept well on leaves because the fevers were gone.

practice: Close your eyes and let the body be heavy, as if already in bed. Bring to mind someone in your house, or someone far away, and wish them a night of good sleep, the way the old practice of metta wishes all beings well and at ease.

wordCard.voice: Sleep: rest that comes when the fevers of wanting, anger and confusion have cooled, whatever the bed is like.

carryVoice: A line for the night: sleep well, with the fever cooled. One of nine, in body, illness and age.

sources.ref: Anguttara Nikaya 3.34 (Hatthaka Sutta: on a cold winter night, the Buddha on a spread of leaves; 'one of those who sleep well'; the householder's fevers of lust, hatred and delusion)
Sutta Nipata 1.8 (Karaniya Metta Sutta: may all beings be happy and at ease)
